BD-22.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask the two divisions of the Supreme Court, retirement age, writ jurisdiction (Art. 102), separation of the judiciary (1 November 2007, Masdar Hossain case), the first Chief Justice and first woman judge, the Ombudsman (Art. 77) and the Anti-Corruption Commission (2004).

## Structure of the judiciary 🔥
- Article **94**: the **Supreme Court of Bangladesh** has two divisions:
  - **আপিল বিভাগ (Appellate Division)** — highest court of appeal.
  - **হাইকোর্ট বিভাগ (High Court Division)** — original (writ) and appellate jurisdiction.
- Headed by the **Chief Justice of Bangladesh (প্রধান বিচারপতি)**, who sits in the Appellate Division.
- Seat: **Dhaka** (Art. 100).
- Judges are appointed by the **President** (Art. 95); the Chief Justice is appointed by the President **on his own** (Art. 48(3)).
- 🔥 Retirement age of Supreme Court judges: **67 years** (raised from 65 by the **14th amendment, 2004**).
- Qualification (Art. 95): citizen, and at least **10 years** as an advocate of the Supreme Court or **10 years** in judicial office (or other qualifications set by law).
- The Supreme Court is a **court of record** (Art. 108) and can punish for **contempt**; its decisions **bind** all lower courts (Art. 111).

### Subordinate courts (অধস্তন আদালত)
- **Civil:** District Judge → Additional District Judge → Joint District Judge → Senior Assistant Judge → Assistant Judge.
- **Criminal:** Sessions Judge → Additional Sessions Judge → Joint Sessions Judge; **Chief Judicial / Metropolitan Magistrate** → Judicial Magistrates.
- Special courts and tribunals: **Administrative Tribunals** (Art. 117) for service matters, Labour Court, Family Courts, etc.
- **Village courts (গ্রাম আদালত)** under the Union Parishad settle small disputes locally.
- **National Legal Aid Services Organization** gives free legal help to poor people (Legal Aid Act 2000).

## Separation of the judiciary 🔥🔥
- Article **22** (a state principle) says the state shall separate the judiciary from the executive.
- 🔥 **মাসদার হোসেন মামলা:** in **1999** the Appellate Division gave a **12-point directive** to separate the lower judiciary from the executive.
- 🔥 The lower judiciary was formally separated on **1 November 2007** (during the caretaker government). Executive magistrates lost their judicial (trial) powers, and **judicial magistrates** took over.

## Removal of judges
- Original 1972 Constitution: removal by **Parliament**.
- Later: the **Supreme Judicial Council (সুপ্রিম জুডিশিয়াল কাউন্সিল)** — the **Chief Justice** and the **two next senior judges** of the Appellate Division — inquires, and the President removes.
- The **16th amendment (2014)** gave this power back to Parliament, but it was declared **unconstitutional** (High Court 2016; Appellate Division 2017), so the **Supreme Judicial Council** system applies.

> 🔄 Update: after 2024, a judiciary reform commission proposed changes (e.g. a separate judicial secretariat and a new process for appointing judges). Check what has been adopted, and check the name of the current Chief Justice.

## Firsts 🔥
| Fact | Answer |
|---|---|
| **First Chief Justice** | **বিচারপতি আবু সাদাত মোহাম্মদ সায়েম** (1972) |
| **First woman judge of the High Court Division** (2000) and of the **Appellate Division** (2011) | **বিচারপতি নাজমুন আরা সুলতানা** |
| Chief Justices who later became President | **A. S. M. Sayem** (1975) and **Shahabuddin Ahmed** (acting 1990–91; elected 1996) |

## Writs (Article 102) — recap 🔥
- The High Court Division can issue **habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto** to enforce fundamental rights (via Art. 44) or to control unlawful public action.
- **Public Interest Litigation (PIL)** is also brought under Article 102.

## Ombudsman (ন্যায়পাল) 🔥
- The word and the institution come from **Sweden** (first Ombudsman **1809**).
- The Ombudsman examines **complaints against public officials and ministries** (maladministration).
- 🔥 In Bangladesh: **Article 77** of the Constitution; the **Ombudsman Act, 1980**.
- 🔥 **No general (parliamentary) Ombudsman has ever been appointed** in Bangladesh.
- A **Tax Ombudsman** was set up under the **Tax Ombudsman Act, 2005** (first appointed in 2006); the office was **abolished in 2011**.

## Anti-Corruption Commission (দুর্নীতি দমন কমিশন, দুদক) 🔥
- Established under the **Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004**; started work on **21 November 2004**.
- It replaced the **Bureau of Anti-Corruption** (দুর্নীতি দমন ব্যুরো).
- An **independent statutory body** (created by law, **not by the Constitution**).
- Three members: a **Chairman** and **two Commissioners**, appointed by the President on the recommendation of a selection committee.
- First Chairman: **বিচারপতি সুলতান হোসেন খান**.
- Headquarters: **Segunbagicha, Dhaka**.

> 🔄 Update: the Anti-Corruption Reform Commission (2024–25) proposed making the ACC a constitutional body and other changes. Check whether this has been adopted.

BD-23.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask the lowest tier (Union Parishad), its members (chairman + 12), the constitutional basis (Art. 59–60), the laws of 2009, the upazila system (1982), the father of local self-government (Lord Ripon) and the number of city corporations.

## Constitutional basis 🔥
- **Article 11**: democracy, with effective participation of the people through elected representatives in administration at all levels.
- 🔥 **Article 59**: local government in every administrative unit shall be entrusted to bodies of **elected persons**.
- **Article 60**: Parliament shall give these bodies powers, including the power to **impose taxes**, prepare budgets and keep funds.
- Ministry: **Local Government Division**, under the **Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives (LGRD)**.

## History (timeline) 🔥
| Year | Step | Key person |
|---|---|---|
| 1870 | **Village Chowkidari Act** — chowkidari panchayat | — |
| 🔥 1882 | Resolution on local self-government — **father of local self-government** | **Lord Ripon** |
| 1885 | **Bengal Local Self-Government Act** — Union Committee, Local Board, District Board | — |
| 1919 | **Bengal Village Self-Government Act** — **Union Board** | — |
| 1959 | **Basic Democracy** — Union Council | Ayub Khan |
| 1973 | Named **Union Parishad** | — |
| 🔥 1982 | Thanas upgraded to **Upazilas** (first upazila elections 1985) | H. M. Ershad |
| 2009 | New laws for Union Parishad, Upazila Parishad, Pourashava and City Corporation | — |

## Rural local government 🔥
### Union Parishad (ইউনিয়ন পরিষদ) — lowest tier 🔥🔥
- The **oldest** and **lowest unit** of local government.
- Law: **Local Government (Union Parishad) Act, 2009**.
- 🔥 Members: **1 Chairman + 9 general ward members + 3 reserved women members = 13**.
- Each union has **9 wards**; each reserved woman member represents **3 wards**.
- Term: **5 years**. The **Secretary (সচিব)** is the government employee who runs the office.
- Runs the **village court (গ্রাম আদালত)**, keeps **birth and death registration**, and handles local development and relief.

### Upazila Parishad (উপজেলা পরিষদ)
- Upazila system started in **1982** (Ershad); first upazila elections **1985**. Abolished in **1991**; revived by the **Upazila Parishad Act 1998** and elections in **2009**.
- 🔥 Directly elected: **1 Chairman + 2 Vice-Chairmen** (one of whom must be a **woman**).
- Union Parishad chairmen and pourashava mayors of the upazila are also members.
- The **Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO)** is the chief executive/secretary of the Parishad.
- Under the 2009 law, the local **MP** is the **adviser** of the Upazila Parishad.

### Zila Parishad (জেলা পরিষদ)
- Law: **Zila Parishad Act, 2000**. The first Zila Parishad elections were held in **December 2016**.
- **Indirectly elected**: chairman and members are elected by the **local government representatives** of the district (UP, upazila and pourashava members).
- Structure: 1 Chairman, **15 general members**, **5 reserved women members**.
- The **three hill districts** have separate **Hill District Councils** (1989) instead.

## Urban local government 🔥
### Pourashava (পৌরসভা, municipality)
- Law: **Local Government (Pourashava) Act, 2009**.
- Headed by an elected **Mayor**, with ward **councillors** and reserved women councillors.
- Classified as **A, B, C** mainly by annual income.
- Dhaka's municipality dates from **1864**.

### City Corporation (সিটি কর্পোরেশন)
- Law: **Local Government (City Corporation) Act, 2009**. Headed by an elected **Mayor**.
- 🔥 **12 city corporations**: **Dhaka North, Dhaka South**, Chattogram, Khulna, Rajshahi, Sylhet, Barishal, Rangpur, Cumilla, Narayanganj, Gazipur, Mymensingh.
- 🔥 Dhaka City Corporation was **split into North and South in 2011**.

## Special system: Chattogram Hill Tracts
| Body | Basis |
|---|---|
| **Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Bandarban Hill District Councils** | Hill District Local Government Council Acts, **1989** |
| **CHT Regional Council (পার্বত্য চট্টগ্রাম আঞ্চলিক পরিষদ)** | **CHT Regional Council Act, 1998**, after the **CHT Accord (1997)** |

## Summary table
| Tier | Head | Law | Election |
|---|---|---|---|
| Union Parishad | Chairman | UP Act 2009 | Direct |
| Upazila Parishad | Chairman (+2 Vice-Chairmen) | Upazila Parishad Act 1998 (amended 2009) | Direct |
| Zila Parishad | Chairman | Zila Parishad Act 2000 | Indirect |
| Pourashava | Mayor | Pourashava Act 2009 | Direct |
| City Corporation | Mayor | City Corporation Act 2009 | Direct |

> 🔄 Update: after August 2024 many elected local government heads (mayors, chairmen) were removed and **administrators** were appointed, and a Local Government Reform Commission proposed changes. The number of unions, upazilas and pourashavas also changes over time (about 495 upazilas and over 4,500 unions as of the early 2020s). Check current figures and the present structure.

BD-24.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask the number of divisions and districts, the newest divisions (Rangpur, Mymensingh), the largest and smallest district, border districts, the administrative hierarchy (DC, UNO), and the CHT Peace Accord (2 December 1997).

## Administrative hierarchy 🔥
| Level | Head |
|---|---|
| **Ministry / Division (Secretariat)** | Minister; **Secretary** (senior-most civil servant: **Cabinet Secretary**) |
| **বিভাগ (Division)** | **Divisional Commissioner (বিভাগীয় কমিশনার)** |
| **জেলা (District)** | 🔥 **Deputy Commissioner (DC, জেলা প্রশাসক)** — also District Magistrate and Collector |
| **উপজেলা (Upazila)** | 🔥 **Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO)** |
| **ইউনিয়ন (Union)** | Union Parishad (elected; see BD-23) |

- The civil service is the **Bangladesh Civil Service (BCS)**, recruited by the **PSC**; there are **26 cadres** (after BCS Economic merged with Administration in 2018).

## Divisions (বিভাগ) 🔥🔥
- 🔥 **8 divisions**, **64 districts**.

| Division | Created | Districts |
|---|---|---|
| **Dhaka** | Old (British period) | **13** (most) |
| **Chattogram** | Old | **11** |
| **Rajshahi** | Old | 8 |
| **Khulna** | 1960 | 10 |
| **Barishal** | **1993** | 6 |
| **Sylhet** | **1995** | 4 |
| 🔥 **Rangpur** | **2010** | 8 |
| 🔥 **Mymensingh** | **2015** — the **newest** division | 4 |
| **Total** | | **64** |

- The present **64 districts** were created in **1984** by upgrading the old sub-divisions (মহকুমা).
- Largest division by area: **Chattogram**; smallest: **Mymensingh**. Most districts: **Dhaka (13)**; fewest: **Sylhet and Mymensingh (4 each)**.

## District facts 🔥
| Fact | Answer |
|---|---|
| **Largest district by area** | 🔥 **Rangamati** |
| **Smallest district by area** | 🔥 **Narayanganj** |
| Districts bordering **Myanmar** | **3**: **Rangamati, Bandarban, Cox's Bazar** |
| Districts bordering **India** | **30** |
| Total **border districts** | **32** (Rangamati touches both India and Myanmar) |
| Area of Bangladesh | **1,47,570 sq km** |

- **Enclave exchange:** under the **1974 Land Boundary Agreement** and its 2011 protocol, **111 Indian enclaves** came to Bangladesh and **51 Bangladeshi enclaves** went to India at midnight on **31 July 2015**.

## Chattogram Hill Tracts (CHT) background
- **Three hill districts**: **Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Bandarban**.
- Home to many ethnic communities; the **Chakma** are the largest group, followed by the Marma and Tripura.
- The **Kaptai dam** (1960s) flooded large areas and displaced many hill people.
- **Parbatya Chattagram Jana Samhati Samiti (PCJSS)** was formed in 1972; its armed wing **শান্তিবাহিনী** fought for autonomy for about two decades.

## CHT Peace Accord 1997 (পার্বত্য চট্টগ্রাম শান্তিচুক্তি) 🔥🔥
- 🔥 **Signed: 2 December 1997**, in Dhaka, during Sheikh Hasina's first government.
- Parties:
  - **Government side:** the **National Committee on CHT**, led by its convener **আবুল হাসনাত আবদুল্লাহ** (Chief Whip).
  - **Hill people's side:** **PCJSS**, led by **জ্যোতিরিন্দ্র বোধিপ্রিয় লারমা (সন্তু লারমা)**.
- No foreign third party was involved (it was a domestic agreement).
- Structure: **4 parts (খণ্ড)** with **72 articles/clauses** in total.
- 🔥 **Shanti Bahini surrendered arms on 10 February 1998** at **Khagrachhari** stadium.
- For this accord, **Sheikh Hasina** received **UNESCO's Félix Houphouët-Boigny Peace Prize (1998)**.

### Main outcomes of the accord
| Outcome | Year |
|---|---|
| **Ministry of Chattogram Hill Tracts Affairs** created | **1998** |
| **CHT Regional Council (আঞ্চলিক পরিষদ)** — Act 1998; chairman **Santu Larma** | 1998 (functioning from 1999) |
| Strengthening of the three **Hill District Councils** | 1998 |
| **Land Dispute Resolution Commission** | 1999 (Act 2001) |
| Withdrawal of temporary army camps; rehabilitation of refugees returning from India | Phased |

- The **UPDF** (United People's Democratic Front) was formed by a group of hill people who **opposed** the accord.

> 🔄 Update: the number of upazilas and some administrative units change over time, and a Public Administration Reform Commission (2024–25) proposed changes (for example on divisions and cadres). Check the latest figures and decisions.

## Quick revision
- **8 divisions, 64 districts**; districts created in **1984**.
- Newest divisions: **Rangpur (2010)**, **Mymensingh (2015)**.
- Barishal **1993**, Sylhet **1995**.
- Most districts: **Dhaka (13)**.
- Largest district: **Rangamati**; smallest: **Narayanganj**.
- Myanmar border districts: **Rangamati, Bandarban, Cox's Bazar**.
- District head: **DC**; upazila head: **UNO**.
- CHT Accord: **2 December 1997**; Abul Hasnat Abdullah and **Santu Larma**.
- Arms surrender: **10 February 1998**, Khagrachhari.
- Enclave exchange: **31 July 2015** (111 to Bangladesh, 51 to India).

BD-25.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Almost every exam asks at least one question on Bangladesh's latitude/longitude, border lengths, border districts, the 2015 enclave exchange or the 2012/2014 maritime verdicts.

## Location (অবস্থান) 🔥
- Latitude: **20°34′ N to 26°38′ N**. Longitude: **88°01′ E to 92°41′ E**.
- The **Tropic of Cancer (কর্কটক্রান্তি রেখা, about 23.5° N)** passes through the **middle** of Bangladesh (west to east through districts such as Jhenaidah, Magura, Faridpur, Cumilla, Khagrachhari and Rangamati).
- Bangladesh Standard Time = **GMT + 6 hours**. The standard meridian is **90° E**.
- Neighbours: **India** on the west, north and east; **Myanmar** on the south-east; the **Bay of Bengal (বঙ্গোপসাগর)** on the south.
- Bangladesh does not touch Nepal or Bhutan. India's narrow **Siliguri corridor ("Chicken's Neck")** separates them.

## Area (আয়তন)
- Official area: **1,47,570 sq km (56,977 sq miles)**. This is the figure used in most textbooks and exams.
- Some recent government publications give **1,48,460 sq km**, adding land gained after the enclave exchange and river-bed changes. If both appear as options, choose **1,47,570 sq km** unless the question says "updated/revised".

## Extreme points (সীমান্ত বিন্দু) 🔥
| Direction | Place |
|---|---|
| Northernmost | **বাংলাবান্ধা, তেঁতুলিয়া, পঞ্চগড়** |
| Southernmost | **ছেঁড়া দ্বীপ** (near St Martin's, Cox's Bazar); southernmost upazila **টেকনাফ** |
| Easternmost | **আখাইনঠং, থানচি, বান্দরবান** |
| Westernmost | **মনাকশা, শিবগঞ্জ, চাঁপাইনবাবগঞ্জ** |

## Borders (সীমানা) 🔥
Two sets of figures are in use. Know both:

| Border | Border Guard Bangladesh / most exam guides | BBS Statistical Yearbook |
|---|---|---|
| With India | **4,156 km** | 3,715 km |
| With Myanmar | **271 km** (some write 283 km) | 280 km |
| Coastline (উপকূল) | **711 km** (some write 710) | 716 km |

- **Indian states touching Bangladesh: 5** — West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram.
  - Longest border: **West Bengal**. Shortest: **Mizoram**.
- **Border districts:** **30 districts** touch India, **3 districts** touch Myanmar (**Rangamati, Bandarban, Cox's Bazar**). **Rangamati** touches both India and Myanmar, so there are **32 border districts** in all.
- The **Naf river (নাফ নদী)** forms part of the Bangladesh–Myanmar border.
- **Divisions with no land border with India:** **Barishal** (coastal) and, since Mymensingh division was carved out in 2015, **Dhaka** division.

## Enclaves (ছিটমহল) exchange 2015 🔥🔥
- **Land Boundary Agreement (স্থল সীমান্ত চুক্তি)** signed **16 May 1974** by **Sheikh Mujibur Rahman** and **Indira Gandhi** (the Mujib–Indira Pact).
- Bangladesh ratified it quickly (**3rd Amendment of the Constitution, 1974**). India did not until **2015**.
- 2011: an additional **Protocol** was signed (Manmohan Singh's Dhaka visit).
- May 2015: India's Parliament passed the **Constitution (100th Amendment) Act**.
- **6 June 2015:** instruments of ratification exchanged in Dhaka (Narendra Modi's visit).
- **Midnight of 31 July 2015 (effective 1 August 2015):** enclaves physically exchanged.

| | Number | Area |
|---|---|---|
| Indian enclaves that became **Bangladeshi** | **111** | **17,160.63 acres** |
| Bangladeshi enclaves that became **Indian** | **51** | **7,110.02 acres** |

- Bangladesh gained about **10,050 acres** net.
- The 111 enclaves were in **Lalmonirhat (59), Panchagarh (36), Kurigram (12), Nilphamari (4)**.
- **দহগ্রাম–আঙ্গরপোতা** (Patgram, Lalmonirhat) remained with Bangladesh. It is linked to the mainland by the **তিনবিঘা করিডোর**, leased from India in **1992** and open **24 hours since 2011**.

## Maritime boundary (সমুদ্রসীমা) 🔥🔥
| Dispute | Tribunal | Verdict date | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bangladesh vs Myanmar** | **ITLOS** (International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea), **Hamburg, Germany** | **14 March 2012** | Bangladesh got about **1,11,631 sq km** of sea area |
| **Bangladesh vs India** | **Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA), The Hague** | **7 July 2014** | Of **25,602 sq km** disputed area, Bangladesh got **19,467 sq km** |

- After both verdicts Bangladesh has about **1,18,813 sq km** of territorial sea, EEZ and continental shelf.
- **South Talpatti (দক্ষিণ তালপট্টি / New Moore)** island, near the Hariabhanga river mouth, fell on India's side; it has since disappeared under the sea.
- Under **UNCLOS 1982**: territorial sea **12 nautical miles**, contiguous zone **24 NM**, **EEZ 200 NM**, continental shelf up to **350 NM** (where the shelf extends).
- Bangladesh's own law: **Territorial Waters and Maritime Zones Act, 1974** (amended 2021).

## Quick revision
- Bangladesh lies between **20°34′–26°38′ N** and **88°01′–92°41′ E**.
- The **Tropic of Cancer** crosses the middle of the country; time zone **GMT+6**.
- Area **1,47,570 sq km** (revised figure 1,48,460 sq km in some sources).
- 5 Indian states border Bangladesh; longest with **West Bengal**, shortest with **Mizoram**.
- 3 districts border Myanmar: **Rangamati, Bandarban, Cox's Bazar**.
- LBA 1974 → implemented **31 July 2015 midnight**: **111** enclaves in, **51** out.
- Myanmar case: **ITLOS, 14 March 2012**; India case: **PCA, 7 July 2014 (19,467 sq km)**.
- Total sea area: **1,18,813 sq km**.

BD-26.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Questions on river origins, confluences, trans-boundary rivers and bridge facts (length, location, opening date) appear in nearly every BCS and bank exam.

## Rivers: basic facts 🔥
- Bangladesh is called **"নদীমাতৃক দেশ"** (land of rivers).
- Number of rivers: traditionally "**about 700**". In **2023** the **National River Conservation Commission (জাতীয় নদী রক্ষা কমিশন)** published a list of **1,008 rivers**. Older BIWTA figure: 230. Use the figure that matches the question's source.
- **Trans-boundary (আন্তঃসীমান্ত) rivers: 57** — **54 with India**, **3 with Myanmar** (**নাফ, সাঙ্গু, মাতামুহুরী** in most guides).
- The **Naf** forms part of the Bangladesh–Myanmar border.

## Major river systems
| River | Key facts |
|---|---|
| **পদ্মা (Padma)** | The Ganges (গঙ্গা) enters at **Chapainawabganj/Rajshahi**; joins the **Jamuna at Goalundo (Rajbari)** and then the **Meghna at Chandpur** |
| **যমুনা (Jamuna)** | Main flow of the **Brahmaputra** (from Tibet, via Assam), enters at **Kurigram**; shifted to the present Jamuna course after the **1787** earthquake/flood |
| **পুরাতন ব্রহ্মপুত্র** | Old course, flows past Mymensingh |
| **মেঘনা (Meghna)** | Formed by the **সুরমা** and **কুশিয়ারা** (both from the **Barak** river of Assam/Manipur); meets the Padma at **Chandpur** and falls into the Bay of Bengal. Often called the **widest** and, in most exam guides, the longest river inside Bangladesh |
| **কর্ণফুলী (Karnaphuli)** | Rises in the **Lushai hills (Mizoram)**; **Chattogram port** is on it; **Kaptai dam** built on it |
| **তিস্তা (Teesta)** | From **Sikkim**; **Teesta Barrage** at **Dalia (Lalmonirhat/Nilphamari)**; water sharing unresolved |
| **হালদা (Halda)** | Chattogram; the only **natural carp breeding ground (রুই জাতীয় মাছের প্রাকৃতিক প্রজনন ক্ষেত্র)** in South Asia; declared **"Bangabandhu Fisheries Heritage"** in 2020 |
| **সাঙ্গু ও হালদা** | Both rise and end inside Bangladesh (exam favourite) |
| **বুড়িগঙ্গা** | Dhaka city stands on its bank |
| **শীতলক্ষ্যা** | Narayanganj |
| **করতোয়া** | Mahasthangarh (Bogura) on its bank |
| **গড়াই–মধুমতী** | Main distributary of the Padma towards the south-west |

- **Longest river (by exam convention):** Meghna. Some sources name the Padma or the Surma, so read the options carefully.
- **Kaptai Lake (কাপ্তাই হ্রদ)** is the **largest artificial lake**, formed by the Kaptai dam (1960s). It feeds the **Karnaphuli Hydro Power Station**, the country's only hydro plant.

## Water treaties 🔥
- **Farakka Barrage (ফারাক্কা বাঁধ)**: on the Ganges in **Murshidabad, West Bengal**; commissioned **21 April 1975**. **Farakka Long March** led by **Maulana Bhashani** on **16 May 1976**.
- **Ganges Water Sharing Treaty (গঙ্গা পানিবণ্টন চুক্তি)**: signed **12 December 1996**, valid for **30 years**, so it **expires in December 2026**. Renewal is a hot current-affairs issue.
- **Joint Rivers Commission (যৌথ নদী কমিশন)** Bangladesh–India: formed **1972**.

## Bridges 🔥🔥
| Bridge | River / place | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| **পদ্মা সেতু (Padma Multipurpose Bridge)** | Padma; **Mawa (Munshiganj)** – **Janjira (Shariatpur)** | **6.15 km**, longest bridge in Bangladesh; **41 spans, 42 pillars**; two-storey (road on top, rail below); built with **own funds**; main contractor **China Major Bridge Engineering Company**; inaugurated **25 June 2022**, open to traffic **26 June 2022**; rail link on the bridge opened **10 October 2023** |
| **যমুনা সেতু (Jamuna Bridge)** — named **Bangabandhu Bridge** in 1998 | Jamuna; **Bhuapur (Tangail) – Sirajganj** | **4.8 km**; opened **23 June 1998**; carries road, rail, gas and power lines. Renamed **Jamuna Bridge** in 2025 |
| **যমুনা রেলসেতু** | Parallel to the Jamuna Bridge | **4.8 km**, country's **longest dedicated rail bridge**; opened to trains in **2025** |
| **হার্ডিঞ্জ ব্রিজ** | Padma; **Paksey (Pabna)** | **Railway bridge, opened 1915** (British era), about **1.8 km** |
| **লালন শাহ সেতু** | Padma; Paksey (Pabna) – Bheramara (Kushtia) | Road bridge, **2004**, next to Hardinge Bridge |
| **সৈয়দ নজরুল ইসলাম সেতু** | Meghna; **Bhairab – Ashuganj** | Road bridge, 2002 |
| **খান জাহান আলী সেতু (Rupsha Bridge)** | Rupsha, **Khulna** | 2005 |
| **শাহ আমানত সেতু** | Karnaphuli, **Chattogram** | 2010 |
| **মৈত্রী সেতু** | **Feni river**; **Ramgarh (Khagrachhari) – Sabroom (Tripura, India)** | Inaugurated **9 March 2021** |
| **পায়রা সেতু (Lebukhali)** | Payra river, **Patuakhali** | 2021 |

- **Memory hook:** Padma **6.15** → Jamuna **4.8** → Hardinge/Lalon Shah about **1.8** km.

> 🔄 Update: bridge and project names have been changed several times since 2024; check the current official name in a newspaper before the exam.

## Quick revision
- 57 trans-boundary rivers: **54 India + 3 Myanmar**.
- Padma + Jamuna meet at **Goalundo**; Padma + Meghna at **Chandpur**.
- Surma + Kushiyara → **Meghna** (both from the **Barak**).
- **Halda** = natural carp breeding ground (Chattogram).
- Farakka commissioned **1975**; Ganges Treaty **12 Dec 1996**, 30 years.
- Padma Bridge **6.15 km**, **Mawa–Janjira**, opened **25 June 2022**.
- Jamuna Bridge **4.8 km**, opened **23 June 1998**.
- Hardinge Bridge (rail) **1915**; Maitree Setu on the **Feni** river, **2021**.

BD-27.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Highest peak, the only coral island, the largest island, Sundarbans facts and the largest haor are classic one-line MCQs in BCS, bank and primary exams.

## Physical divisions of Bangladesh 🔥
| Type | Share of land | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Tertiary hills (টারশিয়ারি যুগের পাহাড়)** | about **12%** | Chittagong Hill Tracts, Sylhet and Mymensingh–Netrokona hills |
| **Pleistocene terraces (প্লাইস্টোসিন কালের সোপান)** | about **8%** | **বরেন্দ্রভূমি (Barind Tract)**, **মধুপুর ও ভাওয়ালের গড়**, **লালমাই পাহাড়** (Cumilla) |
| **Recent floodplains (সাম্প্রতিক প্লাবনভূমি)** | about **80%** | Most of the country |

- **Barind Tract:** Rajshahi, Naogaon, Chapainawabganj, Dinajpur, Rangpur, Joypurhat, Bogura area; red, clay soil; drought-prone.
- **Madhupur Tract:** Tangail, Mymensingh; **Bhawal Garh:** Gazipur.

## Hills and peaks 🔥
| Peak / hill | Height / location | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **তাজিংডং (বিজয়)** | about **1,231 m (some write 1,280 m)**, **Bandarban** | **Officially the highest peak** |
| **কেওক্রাডং** | about **986 m**, Ruma, Bandarban | Formerly taught as highest |
| **সাকা হাফং (মদক মুয়াল)** | Thanchi, Bandarban | Some private surveys say it is actually the highest; the exam answer remains **Tajingdong** |
| **Garo hills** | North of Mymensingh–Netrokona–Sherpur | |
| **Lalmai–Mainamati** | Cumilla | Pleistocene hills; archaeological sites |
| **Chimbuk (চিম্বুক)** | Bandarban | Tourist hill |

- The highest hill range is the **Modhok (Mowdok) range** in Bandarban.
- Bandarban is the district with the most high peaks.

## Islands (দ্বীপ) 🔥
| Island | District | Key fact |
|---|---|---|
| **সেন্টমার্টিন (নারিকেল জিঞ্জিরা / দারুচিনি দ্বীপ)** | Teknaf, **Cox's Bazar** | **Only coral island** of Bangladesh; declared an **Ecologically Critical Area (1999)** |
| **ছেঁড়া দ্বীপ** | Cox's Bazar | Southernmost point of Bangladesh |
| **ভোলা (দক্ষিণ শাহবাজপুর)** | Bhola | **Largest island**; an island district |
| **মহেশখালী** | Cox's Bazar | **Only hilly island**; Adinath temple |
| **সন্দ্বীপ** | Chattogram | Old island in the Meghna estuary |
| **হাতিয়া** | Noakhali | |
| **নিঝুম দ্বীপ** | Hatiya, Noakhali | Famous for **spotted deer (চিত্রা হরিণ)**; national park **2001** |
| **কুতুবদিয়া** | Cox's Bazar | Lighthouse; wind power pilot plant |
| **সোনাদিয়া** | Cox's Bazar | Mangrove and migratory birds |
| **ভাসানচর** | Noakhali | Rohingya relocation site since **December 2020** |
| **মনপুরা, চর কুকরি-মুকরি** | Bhola | |
| **দুবলার চর** | Inside the Sundarbans | Dry fish; **রাস মেলা** |

## The Sundarbans (সুন্দরবন) 🔥🔥
- The **largest single mangrove forest (ম্যানগ্রোভ বন)** in the world.
- Total area about **10,000 sq km**; about **6,017 sq km (about 62%)** lies in Bangladesh, the rest in India (West Bengal).
- Districts: **Khulna, Bagerhat, Satkhira** (some sources add parts of Patuakhali and Barguna).
- Name: from the **সুন্দরী গাছ (Heritiera fomes)**. Other trees: গেওয়া, গরান, কেওড়া, গোলপাতা.
- **UNESCO World Heritage Site:** **6 December 1997** (the Bangladesh part is the **798th** site on the list).

- **Tiger census:** **114** (2018); **125** (survey result published in **2024**).

BD-28.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask about the type of climate, the six seasons and their Bangla months, the wettest/driest places, record temperatures, Kalbaishakhi and cyclone signals.

## Type of climate 🔥
- Bangladesh has a **tropical monsoon climate (ক্রান্তীয় মৌসুমি জলবায়ু)**: hot, humid summers, heavy summer rain and mild, dry winters.
- The **south-west monsoon (দক্ষিণ-পশ্চিম মৌসুমি বায়ু)** brings most of the rain (June–October).
- The **north-east wind** blows in winter and is dry.
- Hottest month: **April**. Coldest month: **January**. Rainiest month: usually **July**.
- Average annual rainfall: exam guides give about **203 cm**; it varies from about 150 cm in the west to over 400 cm in the north-east.

## Six seasons (ষড়ঋতু) 🔥🔥
| Season | Bangla months | Approx. English months |
|---|---|---|
| **গ্রীষ্ম (Summer)** | **বৈশাখ – জ্যৈষ্ঠ** | mid-April – mid-June |
| **বর্ষা (Rainy)** | **আষাঢ় – শ্রাবণ** | mid-June – mid-August |
| **শরৎ (Autumn)** | **ভাদ্র – আশ্বিন** | mid-August – mid-October |
| **হেমন্ত (Late autumn)** | **কার্তিক – অগ্রহায়ণ** | mid-October – mid-December |
| **শীত (Winter)** | **পৌষ – মাঘ** | mid-December – mid-February |
| **বসন্ত (Spring)** | **ফাল্গুন – চৈত্র** | mid-February – mid-April |

- **Memory hook:** গ্রী–ব–শ–হে–শী–ব (each season = 2 months).
- **Revised Bangla calendar** (Bangla Academy): **1 Baishakh = 14 April** every year.
- **Climatically** (Meteorological Department) there are **3 seasons**: **summer (March–May)**, **rainy season (June–October)**, **winter (November–February)**.

## Extremes and records 🔥
| Fact | Answer |
|---|---|
| Place with the **highest rainfall** | **লালাখাল, Jaintiapur (Sylhet)**; Sylhet region is the wettest |
| Place with the **lowest rainfall** | **লালপুর (Natore)** |
| **Lowest recorded temperature** | **2.8 °C at Srimangal (Moulvibazar), 4 January 1968** |
| **Highest recorded temperature** | **45.1 °C at Rajshahi, 30 May 1972** |
| Hottest region | North-west (Rajshahi, Chuadanga, Jashore belt) |
| Coldest region | North (Panchagarh–Tetulia) and Srimangal |

> 🔄 Update: new temperature records are sometimes set (heatwaves of 2023–2024, cold waves in Tetulia); check the latest Meteorological Department report.

## Storms and disasters 🔥
- **কালবৈশাখী (Nor'wester):** violent thunderstorm in **March–May**, coming from the **north-west**.
- **Tornado:** the **Saturia–Manikganj tornado (26 April 1989)** is regarded as the deadliest tornado in world history.
- **Cyclone season:** April–May and October–November.

| Cyclone | Date | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Bhola cyclone** | **12 November 1970** | Deadliest; about **5 lakh** deaths |
| **1991 cyclone** | **29 April 1991** | Chattogram coast; about 1.4 lakh deaths |
| **সিডর (Sidr)** | **15 November 2007** | South-west coast, Sundarbans |
| **আইলা (Aila)** | **25 May 2009** | Khulna–Satkhira |
| **আম্ফান (Amphan)** | **20 May 2020** | Super cyclone |
| **মোখা (Mocha)** | **May 2023** | Cox's Bazar–Myanmar coast |
| **রেমাল (Remal)** | **26 May 2024** | Khulna–Barishal coast |

- Cyclone names come from a list of the **WMO/ESCAP Panel on Tropical Cyclones**; each member country proposes names.

### Cyclone warning signals (sea ports)
| Signal | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 1–2 | Distant cautionary / distant warning (দূরবর্তী সতর্ক সংকেত) |
| 3 | Local cautionary |
| 4 | **Local warning (স্থানীয় হুঁশিয়ারি সংকেত)** |
| 5–7 | **Danger (বিপদ সংকেত)** |
| 8–10 | **Great danger (মহাবিপদ সংকেত)** |
| 11 | **Communication failure (যোগাযোগ বিচ্ছিন্ন)** |

### Floods
- Major floods: **1988**, **1998** (longest-lasting), 2004, 2007, Sylhet 2022, and the **August 2024** eastern flood (Feni, Noakhali, Cumilla).
- **Flash floods (আকস্মিক বন্যা)** hit the haor region in April–May.

## Institutions
- **Bangladesh Meteorological Department (আবহাওয়া অধিদপ্তর)**: Agargaon, Dhaka; runs the Storm Warning Centre.
- **SPARRSO** (Space Research and Remote Sensing Organization): satellite weather images.
- **Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre (FFWC)**: under the Bangladesh Water Development Board.

## Quick revision
- Climate: **tropical monsoon**.
- 6 seasons × 2 months; **শরৎ = ভাদ্র–আশ্বিন**, **হেমন্ত = কার্তিক–অগ্রহায়ণ**.
- 3 climatic seasons: summer, rainy, winter.
- Highest rainfall **Lalakhal (Sylhet)**; lowest **Lalpur (Natore)**.
- Record low **2.8 °C Srimangal (1968)**; record high **45.1 °C Rajshahi (1972)**.
- Kalbaishakhi comes from the **north-west** in **March–May**.
- Signal **8–10 = great danger**; **11 = communication cut**.
- Deadliest cyclone: **12 November 1970**.

BD-29.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Every exam has 2–4 questions on the latest budget size, GDP growth, per capita income, the Economic Review and budget "firsts". The numbers change every year, so learn the pattern and update the figures.

## Basics 🔥
- **Fiscal year (অর্থবছর):** **1 July – 30 June**.
- **Bangladesh Economic Review (বাংলাদেশ অর্থনৈতিক সমীক্ষা):** published by the **Finance Division, Ministry of Finance**, every year **just before the budget** (usually early June). It reviews the outgoing year. Sources of its data: **BBS**, Bangladesh Bank, NBR, EPB.
- **GDP and per-capita figures** come from the **Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS)**, established **1974**. Current **base year: 2015–16** (changed from 2005–06 in 2021).
- **Constitution:** the budget is the **"Annual Financial Statement" (বার্ষিক আর্থিক বিবৃতি)** under **Article 87**; money bills under **Article 81**.
- **Bangladesh Bank** (central bank): established **16 December 1971** (Bangladesh Bank Order, 1972, with effect from that date). Currency **Taka** introduced **4 March 1972**.
- **NBR (জাতীয় রাজস্ব বোর্ড)**: 1972. Largest source of tax revenue: **VAT (মূল্য সংযোজন কর)**.

## Income status 🔥
- **Lower-middle-income country** (World Bank) from **1 July 2015**.
- **LDC graduation:** UN CDP recommended it in **February 2021**; UN General Assembly adopted it in **November 2021**; graduation is scheduled for **24 November 2026**. Bangladesh met all three criteria — **per capita GNI, Human Assets Index (HAI), Economic Vulnerability Index (EVI)** — in 2018 and again in 2021.

| GDP growth FY2024–25 | **3.97%** (provisional) | BBS, May 2025 |
| Per capita income FY2024–25 | **US$ 2,820** (provisional) | BBS |
| Poverty rate | **18.7%** (extreme 5.6%) | HIES 2022, BBS |
| Remittance FY2024–25 | about **US$ 30 billion** — a record | Bangladesh Bank |
| Largest export item | **Readymade garments (RMG)**, over 80% of exports | EPB |
| Largest single export market | **USA** (EU as a bloc is larger) | EPB |
| Largest import source | **China** | Bangladesh Bank |

- Sector shares of GDP (approx.): **services about 51–52%**, **industry about 34–37%**, **agriculture about 11–12%**. Agriculture still employs about **45%** of workers (Labour Force Survey 2022).

## Budget FY2025–26 🔥🔥
- Size: **Tk 7,90,000 crore** — the **first budget smaller than the previous year's** (FY2024–25: Tk 7,97,000 crore).
- Presented on **2 June 2025** by **Finance Adviser Dr Salehuddin Ahmed** of the interim government, **through television** (no parliament was sitting), and passed by **ordinance**.

## Agriculture at a glance 🔥
- Agriculture (crops, livestock, fisheries, forestry) is about **11–12% of GDP** but employs about **45% of the workforce** (Labour Force Survey 2022).
- **Main crop:** **rice (ধান)**. Bangladesh is commonly cited as the **3rd largest rice producer** (after China and India).
- **Jute:** **2nd largest producer** (after India) and the **largest exporter of raw jute**. Jute is called the **"সোনালি আঁশ" (golden fibre)**.
- **Hilsa:** Bangladesh produces the largest share of the world's hilsa (ইলিশ).
- **National Agriculture Day (জাতীয় কৃষি দিবস / নবান্ন):** **1 Agrahayan**. **National Jute Day:** **6 March**. **National Tea Day:** **4 June**.

| **রবি (Rabi)** | Kartik–Falgun (about Oct–Mar), dry winter | **Boro rice**, wheat, potato, mustard, lentil, onion |
| **খরিফ-১ (Kharif-1)** | Chaitra–Jaistha (about Mar–Jun) | **Aus rice**, jute |
| **খরিফ-২ (Kharif-2)** | Asharh–Ashwin (about Jun–Oct) | **Aman rice** |

- Three rice crops: **আউশ, আমন, বোরো**. **Boro gives the largest production** today; Aman covers a large area and is the traditional main crop.
- Wheat grows mostly in the north (Dinajpur, Rangpur, Rajshahi).

> **Why it matters:** RMG firsts, Rana Plaza, Adamjee Jute Mills, the list of EPZs and the location of special economic zones are frequent MCQs in BCS and bank exams.

## Readymade garments (তৈরি পোশাক শিল্প, RMG) 🔥🔥
- RMG earns **over 80%** of Bangladesh's export income. Bangladesh is the **2nd largest garment exporter** in the world after **China** (Vietnam is close behind).
- **Pioneers:** **Reaz Garments** (Riaz Uddin) made the **first export shipment (1978, to France)**. **Desh Garments** (Nurul Quader Khan, 1978–79) was the first **100% export-oriented** joint venture, with **Daewoo (South Korea)**.
- Trade bodies: **BGMEA** (woven garments, 1983) and **BKMEA** (knitwear).
- **Tazreen Fashions fire:** **24 November 2012**, Ashulia.
- **Rana Plaza collapse:** **24 April 2013**, **Savar**; more than **1,100** workers died — the worst disaster in the garment industry. It led to the **Accord** (European buyers) and the **Alliance** (North American buyers) on factory safety.
- **Green factories:** Bangladesh has the **highest number of LEED-certified green garment factories in the world** (US Green Building Council).
- Main markets: **EU** (as a bloc) and the **USA** (as a single country).
- Minimum wage for garment workers was last revised in **2023** (Tk 12,500).

> 🔄 Update: check the latest RMG export figure and minimum wage in a newspaper or the Bangladesh Economic Review.

## Jute industry (পাট শিল্প) 🔥
- **Adamjee Jute Mills**, **Siddhirganj, Narayanganj** (1951) was the **largest jute mill in the world**. It closed on **30 June 2002**. The site is now **Adamjee EPZ**.
- **BJMC** (Bangladesh Jute Mills Corporation) stopped production in its state-owned mills in **July 2020**.
- **Mandatory Jute Packaging Act, 2010**: jute bags compulsory for many products.
- **Jute Research Institute:** Dhaka (see BD-30). **Jute Day:** 6 March.

## EPZs (রপ্তানি প্রক্রিয়াকরণ এলাকা) 🔥🔥

> **Why it matters:** "Which is the first/largest gas field?", "Where is the only coal mine?", "Where is white clay found?" — these location-type questions repeat in almost every exam.

## Natural gas (প্রাকৃতিক গ্যাস) 🔥🔥
- Natural gas is Bangladesh's **main commercial energy source**; mostly **methane**. The **largest user is the power sector**.
- **First gas field discovered:** **হরিপুর, Sylhet (1955)**.
- **First gas production:** **ছাতক (1957/1960)**, supplied to the Chhatak cement factory.
- **Largest gas field by reserves:** **তিতাস (Brahmanbaria)**, discovered **1962**.
- **Largest producer today:** **বিবিয়ানা (Habiganj)**, operated by **Chevron**.
- **First offshore gas field:** **সাঙ্গু** (Bay of Bengal, discovered 1996); production has stopped.
- **Bhola:** **শাহবাজপুর** gas field (1995) and later fields in Bhola.
- **Total gas fields:** **29** according to Petrobangla (older books say 26–28).
- **National Energy Security Day (জাতীয় জ্বালানি নিরাপত্তা দিবস):** **9 August**. On **9 August 1975** the government bought **5 gas fields** from **Shell**: **Titas, Bakhrabad, Habiganj, Rashidpur, Kailashtila**.
- **LNG import** began in **2018** through a floating terminal (FSRU) at **Moheshkhali, Cox's Bazar**.

## Oil (খনিজ তেল)
- **Only oil field:** **হরিপুর, Sylhet** (discovered **1986**); production stopped in the 1990s.
- **Only refinery:** **Eastern Refinery**, Patenga, Chattogram (**1968**).

BD-33.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Rooppur (location, capacity, partner country), the only hydro plant, big coal plants and solar/wind "firsts" are regular MCQs; installed-capacity figures appear in written and viva too.

## Power sector basics 🔥
- Main fuel for electricity: **natural gas**; then furnace oil, coal, imports, and a small share of renewables.
- **100% electricity coverage** was declared on **21 March 2022** (at the Payra plant).
- Installed capacity (grid, including imports and renewables) passed **25,000 MW in 2022** and was about **27,000–28,000 MW by 2024**; actual generation is much lower because of fuel shortages. Figures differ by source.

> 🔄 Update: check the latest installed capacity and peak generation record in a newspaper or the Bangladesh Economic Review.

### Institutions
| Body | Role |
|---|---|
| **BPDB** – Bangladesh Power Development Board (**1972**) | Main generation and planning body |
| **PGCB** – Power Grid Company of Bangladesh (1996) | National transmission grid |
| **REB** – Rural Electrification Board (**1977**) | Rural supply through **Palli Bidyut Samities** |
| **DPDC, DESCO** | Dhaka distribution |
| **BERC** – Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (**2003**) | Sets electricity and gas prices |
| **SREDA** – Sustainable and Renewable Energy Development Authority (**2014**) | Promotes renewables and efficiency |
| **BAEC** – Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission (**1973**) | Nuclear science; runs the **TRIGA Mark II research reactor** at **Savar** (1986) |

## Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant (রূপপুর পারমাণবিক বিদ্যুৎকেন্দ্র) 🔥🔥
- Location: **Rooppur, Ishwardi, Pabna**, on the bank of the **Padma**.
- Capacity: **2 units × 1,200 MW = 2,400 MW**.
- Reactor type: **VVER-1200** (Russian, Generation III+).
- Built by **Rosatom** (Russia) with a Russian state loan of about **US$ 11.38 billion**.
- First concrete: **Unit 1 on 30 November 2017**, **Unit 2 on 14 July 2018**.
- **Nuclear fuel handed over: 5 October 2023** — Bangladesh became the **33rd country** with nuclear power generation capability.
- The idea dates back to **1961** (Pakistan period).

> 🔄 Update: check whether Unit 1 has started supplying power to the grid and the date.

## Major power plants 🔥
| Plant | Place | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Karnaphuli Hydro Power Station (Kaptai)** | Rangamati | **Only hydro** plant, **230 MW**, started **1962** |
| **Payra Thermal Power Plant** | Kalapara, **Patuakhali** | **1,320 MW** coal; **ultra-supercritical**; Bangladesh–China joint venture |
| **Maitree Super Thermal (Rampal)** | **Bagerhat** | **1,320 MW** coal; Bangladesh–India joint venture (BIFPCL) |
| **Matarbari** | Moheshkhali, **Cox's Bazar** | **1,200 MW** coal; **JICA** funding |
| **Barapukuria** | Dinajpur | Only plant using **local coal** |
| **Ghorasal** | Narsingdi | Oldest large gas-based complex |

### Power import 🔥
- From **India**: first through the **Bheramara (Kushtia) HVDC** link (**2013**); also from Tripura, and from the **Adani Godda plant (Jharkhand)** from **2023**.
- From **Nepal**: first power import through the Indian grid began in **November 2024** (40 MW, trilateral deal).

## Renewable energy (নবায়নযোগ্য জ্বালানি) 🔥
- Renewables are still a small share of generation (about **4–5%** of capacity).
- **Solar Home Systems (SHS):** run by **IDCOL**; one of the **largest off-grid solar programmes in the world** (about 6 million systems).
- **Largest solar park:** **Teesta Solar Park, Sundarganj, Gaibandha (200 MW)**, 2023.
- **First grid-connected solar park:** **Sarishabari, Jamalpur (3 MW)**, 2017.
- **Wind:** pilot plants at **Sonagazi (Feni)** and **Kutubdia**; a larger wind farm at **Khurushkul, Cox's Bazar (60 MW)**.
- **Biogas** and **solar irrigation pumps** are growing in rural areas.
- **Renewable Energy Policy 2025** set targets of **20% by 2030** and **30% by 2040** (earlier policies: 10% target in the 2008 policy).

> 🔄 Update: verify the renewable targets and the largest solar/wind projects in the latest SREDA or newspaper report.

## Quick revision
- 100% electricity coverage: **21 March 2022**.
- Rooppur: **Ishwardi, Pabna**; **2,400 MW**; **VVER-1200**; **Russia/Rosatom**.
- Fuel handover **5 Oct 2023** → **33rd** nuclear-power nation.
- Only hydro plant: **Kaptai, 230 MW (1962)**.
- Payra (China JV), Rampal (India JV), Matarbari (JICA): all coal.
- Largest solar park: **Teesta Solar, Gaibandha (200 MW)**.
- Research reactor: **TRIGA Mark II, Savar (1986)**.

## Dhaka Metro Rail (মেট্রোরেল) 🔥🔥
- Operator: **DMTCL** – Dhaka Mass Transit Company Limited (formed **2013**). Main funder: **JICA (Japan)**.

## Karnaphuli Tunnel (কর্ণফুলী টানেল) 🔥🔥
- The **first underwater road tunnel in South Asia**.
- Opened with the official name **Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman Tunnel**; commonly called the **Karnaphuli Tunnel**.
- Links **Patenga (city side)** with **Anwara (south bank)**, Chattogram, under the **Karnaphuli river**.
- Length: about **3.32 km** (each tunnel tube about **2.45 km**), plus approach roads.
- Built by **China Communications Construction Company (CCCC)** with a Chinese loan.
- Inaugurated on **28 October 2023**.
- Idea: **"One City, Two Towns"**, like Shanghai.

- Place: **Matarbari, Moheshkhali, Cox's Bazar**.
- **Matarbari coal power plant:** **1,200 MW** (2 × 600 MW), ultra-supercritical, funded by **JICA**, run by CPGCBL.
- **Matarbari Deep Sea Port:** Bangladesh's **first deep-sea port**, under construction with **Japanese (JICA)** support. The channel was first dug to bring coal ships to the power plant. It will let large ships dock directly.

> **Why it matters:** "Which group is matrilineal?", "Where do the Santals live?", "What is Boisabi?" and CHT Peace Accord questions come up in BCS, primary and NTRCA exams regularly.

## Legal status and numbers 🔥
- **Article 23A** of the Constitution (added by the **15th Amendment, 2011**) says the state will protect the culture of **"উপজাতি, ক্ষুদ্র জাতিসত্তা, নৃ-গোষ্ঠী ও সম্প্রদায়"**.
- **Small Ethnic Groups Cultural Institutions Act, 2010 (ক্ষুদ্র নৃ-গোষ্ঠীর সাংস্কৃতিক প্রতিষ্ঠান আইন ২০১০)**.
- A government gazette (**2019**) lists **50 ethnic groups**.
- **Census 2022:** ethnic population **16,50,159** (about **1%** of the population).
- **Largest group: চাকমা (Chakma)**; second **মারমা (Marma)**. The largest group in the **plain lands** is the **সাঁওতাল (Santal)**.

| **মারমা** | **Bandarban**, Khagrachhari | **Buddhist** | Festival **সাংগ্রাই**; **Bohmong Circle** (Bandarban) and **Mong Circle** (Khagrachhari) chiefs are Marma |

- **Matrilineal groups (মাতৃসূত্রীয়): গারো ও খাসিয়া** — the most asked fact.
- **বৈসাবি (Boisabi)** = **বৈ**সু (Tripura) + **সা**ংগ্রাই (Marma) + **বি**জু (Chakma): the hill new-year festival, held at the end of Chaitra / start of Baishakh.

## Chittagong Hill Tracts (পার্বত্য চট্টগ্রাম) 🔥🔥
- Three hill districts: **Rangamati, Khagrachhari, Bandarban**.
- Three traditional **circles**: **Chakma** (Rangamati), **Bohmong** (Bandarban), **Mong** (Khagrachhari).
- **CHT Peace Accord (পার্বত্য চট্টগ্রাম শান্তিচুক্তি):** signed on **2 December 1997** between the Government (National Committee on CHT, convener **Abul Hasnat Abdullah**) and the **PCJSS (পার্বত্য চট্টগ্রাম জনসংহতি সমিতি)** led by **Jyotirindra Bodhipriya Larma (Santu Larma)**.
- Results of the accord: **Ministry of CHT Affairs (1998)**, **CHT Regional Council (1998)** (chairman Santu Larma), **CHT Land Dispute Resolution Commission (2001)**.
- **Hill District Councils** were created earlier, in **1989**.
- **Shanti Bahini** (armed wing of PCJSS) surrendered arms in **February 1998** at Khagrachhari.

## Culture and institutions
- **Small Ethnic Groups Cultural Institutes** exist at Rangamati, Bandarban, Khagrachhari, Birishiri (Netrokona), Rajshahi and elsewhere.
- **9 August:** the UN's **International Day of the World's Indigenous Peoples**. The Government of Bangladesh officially uses the term **ক্ষুদ্র নৃগোষ্ঠী**, not "adivasi".

- Largest: **Chakma**; largest in plains: **Santal**.
- Matrilineal: **Garo, Khasi**.
- Boisabi = **Boisu + Sangrai + Biju**.
- Garo festival **Wangala**; Santal **Sohrai**; Manipuri **Ras**.
- Peace Accord **2 December 1997** with **PCJSS (Santu Larma)**.
- Article **23A** (15th Amendment).

## Festivals (উৎসব) 🔥
- **পহেলা বৈশাখ (Bengali New Year, 14 April):** The Bangla year (**বঙ্গাব্দ / ফসলি সন**) was introduced under Emperor **Akbar** for revenue collection; the calendar was worked out by **আমির ফতেউল্লাহ সিরাজী**. Traders open new account books (**হালখাতা**).
  - **ছায়ানট** has held its dawn programme under the **রমনা বটমূল** since **1967**.
  - The **Mangal Shobhajatra (মঙ্গল শোভাযাত্রা)**, started in **1989** by the **Faculty of Fine Arts (চারুকলা), University of Dhaka**, was inscribed by **UNESCO** as intangible cultural heritage on **30 November 2016**. In **2025** the procession was renamed **"বর্ষবরণ আনন্দ শোভাযাত্রা"**.
- **নবান্ন:** harvest festival on **1 Agrahayan** (also National Agriculture Day).
- **বৈসাবি:** new-year festival of the hill peoples (see BD-38).
- **Ekushey Book Fair (অমর একুশে গ্রন্থমেলা):** every February at **Bangla Academy** (and Suhrawardy Udyan). Started on **8 February 1972** by **চিত্তরঞ্জন সাহা** (Muktadhara) with a few books on a mat; Bangla Academy took charge in **1978**; named "অমর একুশে গ্রন্থমেলা" in **1984**.
- Religious festivals: Eid-ul-Fitr, Eid-ul-Azha, **Durga Puja** (biggest Hindu festival), **Buddha Purnima**, Christmas.
- **রাস মেলা:** Dublar Char (Sundarbans).

BD-40.notes:
> **Why it matters:** The three World Heritage Sites, who built Paharpur, Shat Gombuj Masjid, Mahasthangarh, Mainamati, Lalbagh Fort and Ahsan Manzil are among the most repeated Bangladesh-affairs MCQs.

## UNESCO World Heritage Sites of Bangladesh 🔥🔥
Bangladesh has **3** World Heritage Sites (2 cultural, 1 natural):

| Site | Type | Year |
|---|---|---|
| **Historic Mosque City of Bagerhat (বাগেরহাটের ঐতিহাসিক মসজিদের শহর)** | Cultural | **1985** |
| **Ruins of the Buddhist Vihara at Paharpur (পাহাড়পুর বৌদ্ধ বিহার)** | Cultural | **1985** |
| **The Sundarbans (সুন্দরবন)** | Natural | **1997** |

## Paharpur — Somapura Mahavihara (সোমপুর মহাবিহার) 🔥
- Location: **Badalgachhi, Naogaon**.
- Built by the **Pala king ধর্মপাল** (late 8th – early 9th century).
- The **largest Buddhist monastery south of the Himalayas**; about **177 monks' cells** around a huge cross-shaped central temple with terracotta plaques.
- First noticed by **Buchanan-Hamilton** in the early 19th century; excavated in the 1920s–30s.

## Bagerhat — Khalifatabad 🔥
- Built by **খান জাহান আলী** in the **15th century**; the old city name was **খলিফাতাবাদ**.
- **ষাট গম্বুজ মসজিদ (Shat Gombuj / Sixty Dome Mosque):** despite the name it has **77 domes** on the roof (81 counting the 4 corner towers) and **60 stone pillars**. It is the **largest medieval mosque** in Bangladesh.
- Also: **Khan Jahan's tomb**, **Nine Dome Mosque**, **Singair Mosque**.

## Other major archaeological sites 🔥🔥
| Site | Place | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| **মহাস্থানগড়** | **Bogura**, on the **Karatoya** | Ancient **পুণ্ড্রনগর**; **oldest city-site** of Bangladesh; **Mahasthan Brahmi inscription** (Maurya period); Govinda Bhita; **বেহুলার বাসরঘর (Gokul Medh)** |
| **ময়নামতি** | **Cumilla**, Lalmai–Mainamati hills | **শালবন বিহার** (built by **Deva king Bhavadeva**), Kotila Mura, Charpatra Mura, Ananda Vihara, Rupban Mura |
| **উয়ারী-বটেশ্বর** | **Belabo–Shibpur, Narsingdi** | About **2,500-year-old fort city**; trade beads and punch-marked coins; excavated by Jahangirnagar University since **2000** |
| **সীতাকোট বিহার** | Nawabganj, Dinajpur | Early Buddhist vihara |
| **ভাসু বিহার** | Bogura | |
| **হলুদ বিহার, জগদ্দল বিহার** | Naogaon | Jagaddala founded by Pala king **রামপাল** |
| **পানাম নগর** | **Sonargaon, Narayanganj** | 19th-century merchants' street; Sonargaon was **ঈশা খাঁ**'s capital |
| **কান্তজীর মন্দির (Kantaji Temple)** | **Kantanagar, Dinajpur** | Finest **terracotta** temple; begun by **Maharaja Pran Nath**, completed by his son **Ramnath** (**1752**) |
| **ছোট সোনা মসজিদ** | **Shibganj, Chapainawabganj** | Built in the time of **Sultan Alauddin Hussain Shah**; "gem of Sultanate architecture" |
| **পুঠিয়া রাজবাড়ি** | Rajshahi | Temples and palace |

## Dhaka's historic buildings 🔥
| Building | Key facts |
|---|---|
| **লালবাগ কেল্লা (Lalbagh Fort)** | Begun **1678** by Prince **Muhammad Azam** (son of Aurangzeb); continued by **Shaista Khan**; left **unfinished** after the death of his daughter **পরী বিবি** (1684). Old name **কেল্লা আওরঙ্গাবাদ** |
| **আহসান মঞ্জিল** | Kumartoli, on the **Buriganga**; built by **Nawab Abdul Ghani** (completed **1872**), named after his son **Khwaja Ahsanullah**; called the **"Pink Palace"**; museum since **1992** |
| **বড় কাটরা** | Built **1644** under **Shah Shuja** |
| **ছোট কাটরা** | Built by **Shaista Khan** (1663) |
| **বিনত বিবির মসজিদ** | **1454**; **oldest surviving mosque in Dhaka** |
| **তারা মসজিদ (Star Mosque)** | Armanitola; decorated with star-shaped mosaic |
| **ঢাকেশ্বরী মন্দির** | **National temple** |
| **কার্জন হল** | University of Dhaka; foundation laid by **Lord Curzon** (1904) |

## Museums 🔥
- **বরেন্দ্র গবেষণা জাদুঘর (Varendra Research Museum), Rajshahi (1910):** the **first museum** of Bangladesh.
- **Bangladesh National Museum**, Shahbag: began as the **Dhaka Museum (1913)**; national museum from **1983**.
- **Liberation War Museum:** opened **22 March 1996** at Segunbagicha; moved to **Agargaon** in **2017**.
- **Folk Art and Crafts Museum:** Sonargaon (founded by Zainul Abedin, 1975).
- **Department of Archaeology (প্রত্নতত্ত্ব অধিদপ্তর)** protects sites.

## Quick revision
- 3 World Heritage Sites: **Bagerhat (1985), Paharpur (1985), Sundarbans (1997)**.
- Paharpur = **Somapura Mahavihara**, **Dharmapala**, Naogaon.
- Shat Gombuj Masjid: **Khan Jahan Ali**, **77 domes**, 60 pillars.
- Mahasthangarh = **Pundranagar**, oldest city, Bogura.
- Shalban Vihara: **Mainamati, Cumilla**.
- Lalbagh Fort: **Prince Azam (1678)**, unfinished after **Pari Bibi**'s death.
- Ahsan Manzil: **Nawab Abdul Ghani**, Pink Palace.
- First museum: **Varendra Research Museum (1910)**.

> **Why it matters:** Flag ratio and design, the anthem's writer and line count, the emblem's elements and the list of national symbols are asked in nearly every job exam, including primary and bank exams.

## Constitution
- **Article 3:** State language — **Bangla**.
- **Article 4:** **National anthem, national flag and national emblem**.
- **Article 5:** Capital — **Dhaka**.

## National anthem (জাতীয় সংগীত) 🔥🔥
- Song: **"আমার সোনার বাংলা, আমি তোমায় ভালোবাসি"**.
- Writer and composer: **রবীন্দ্রনাথ ঠাকুর**; written in **1905** during the movement against the **Partition of Bengal (বঙ্গভঙ্গ)**.
- The full song has **25 lines**; the **first 10 lines** are the national anthem.
- The tune is based on the Baul song **"আমি কোথায় পাব তারে"** by **গগন হরকরা**.
- Declared as the anthem on **3 March 1971** (Paltan meeting of the Swadhin Bangla Chhatra Sangram Parishad); officially adopted by the government on **13 January 1972**.
- English translation: **সৈয়দ আলী আহসান**.
- Instrumental version: first **4 lines**.

## National march song (রণসংগীত) 🔥
- **"চল্‌ চল্‌ চল্‌, ঊর্ধ্বগগনে বাজে মাদল"** by **কাজী নজরুল ইসলাম** (from **"সন্ধ্যা"**).
- The first **21 lines** are used. Adopted on **13 January 1972**.

## National flag (জাতীয় পতাকা) 🔥🔥
- A **red circle** on a **dark green** rectangle.
  - Green = youthfulness and the green land; red = the **blood of the martyrs** and the rising sun.
- **Ratio length : width = 10 : 6 (5 : 3)**.
- **Radius of the circle = 1/5 of the length**.
- The centre of the circle is placed at **9/20 of the length from the pole side** (slightly towards the pole), on the middle line of the width.
- **First hoisted:** **2 March 1971** at the **Kala Bhaban, University of Dhaka**, by **আ স ম আবদুর রব** (the original flag had a yellow map in the red circle, designed by **শিব নারায়ণ দাশ**).
- The map was removed and the **final design** by **পটুয়া কামরুল হাসান** was adopted on **17 January 1972**.
- Rules: **Bangladesh Flag Rules, 1972 (পতাকা বিধিমালা)**.

| Use | Sizes |
|---|---|
| Buildings | 10′ × 6′, 5′ × 3′, 2½′ × 1½′ |
| Cars | 15″ × 9″, 10″ × 6″ |
| Table (for meetings) | 10″ × 6″ |

## National emblem (জাতীয় প্রতীক) 🔥🔥
- A **শাপলা (water lily)** floating on **water**,
- bordered on both sides by **ears of paddy (ধানের শীষ)**,
- with **three connected jute leaves (পাটপাতা)** above it,
- and **two stars on each side** of the leaves (**4 stars** in all).

## National Memorial (জাতীয় স্মৃতিসৌধ) 🔥
- At **Nabinagar, Savar, Dhaka**; architect **সৈয়দ মাইনুল হোসেন**.
- Foundation stone laid on **16 December 1972**; completed in **1982**.
- Height **150 feet (45.72 m)**; made of **7 pairs of triangular walls**, representing seven stages of the independence struggle (**1952, 1954, 1956, 1962, 1966, 1969, 1971**).

## Central Shaheed Minar (কেন্দ্রীয় শহীদ মিনার)
- Near Dhaka Medical College; designed by **হামিদুর রহমান** (with **নভেরা আহমেদ**).
- The mother figure with fallen sons; the red sun behind.

- Anthem: **Rabindranath**, **1905**, first **10 lines** of 25; adopted **13 Jan 1972**.
- March song: **Nazrul's "Chol Chol Chol"**, **21 lines**.
- Flag ratio **10:6**; circle radius **1/5** of length; final design **Quamrul Hassan**, adopted **17 Jan 1972**.
- First flag hoisted **2 March 1971**, DU, by **ASM Abdur Rab**.
- Emblem: **water lily, paddy, 3 jute leaves, 4 stars**.
- National tree **mango**; fruit **jackfruit**; bird **doyel**; game **kabaddi**.
- Memorial: **Syed Mainul Hossain**, **7 pairs** of walls, **150 ft**.

BD-43.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Dates of joining international bodies, SAARC and BIMSTEC founding facts, and Bangladesh's UN peacekeeping record are asked in almost every BCS and bank exam.

## Joining international organisations 🔥🔥
| Organisation | Bangladesh joined |
|---|---|
| **Commonwealth** | **18 April 1972** |
| **IMF & World Bank** | **1972** |
| **Non-Aligned Movement (NAM)** | **1973** (Algiers summit) |
| **Asian Development Bank** | **1973** |
| **OIC** | **1974** (**2nd OIC summit, Lahore**, February 1974) |
| **United Nations** | **17 September 1974** — the **136th member** |
| **SAARC** | Founding member, **1985** |
| **D-8** | Founding member, **1997** |
| **BIMSTEC** | Founding member, **1997** |
| **IORA** (Indian Ocean Rim Association) | Member |

## Bangladesh in the United Nations 🔥🔥
- Membership: **17 September 1974**, **136th** member.
- **Sheikh Mujibur Rahman** gave the first **speech in Bangla at the UN General Assembly** on **25 September 1974** (29th session).
- **UN Security Council (non-permanent member):** **1979–80** and **2000–01**.
- **President of the UN General Assembly:** **হুমায়ুন রশীদ চৌধুরী**, **41st session (1986)**.
- **International Mother Language Day:** UNESCO declared **21 February** on **17 November 1999**; observed worldwide from **2000**.
- **UNESCO Memory of the World Register:** the **7 March 1971 speech** (inscribed **30 October 2017**).

## OIC (ইসলামি সহযোগিতা সংস্থা) 🔥
- Founded **1969** (Rabat); secretariat **Jeddah, Saudi Arabia**; **57** members.
- Bangladesh joined in **1974** at the **Lahore summit**; Pakistan recognised Bangladesh (**22 February 1974**) at the same time.
- OIC institution in Bangladesh: **Islamic University of Technology (IUT)**, **Board Bazar, Gazipur**.

## SAARC (সার্ক) 🔥🔥
- Idea proposed by **President Ziaur Rahman** (**1980**).
- Founded on **8 December 1985** at the **first summit in Dhaka**. **8 December = SAARC Charter Day**.
- **8 members:** Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and **Afghanistan** (the **8th**, joined **2007**).
- Secretariat: **Kathmandu, Nepal** (1987). **First Secretary-General: আবুল আহসান (Bangladesh)**.
- **SAFTA** (South Asian Free Trade Area): signed **2004** (Islamabad), in force from **2006**.
- The last summit was the **18th (Kathmandu, 2014)**; the 19th (Islamabad, 2016) was postponed and SAARC has been largely inactive since.

## BIMSTEC (বিমসটেক) 🔥🔥
- Full name: **Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation**.
- Founded on **6 June 1997**, **Bangkok** (as BIST-EC).
- **7 members:** **Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Thailand** (5 South Asian + 2 South-East Asian).
- **Permanent Secretariat: Dhaka** (Gulshan), opened **2014**.
- **BIMSTEC Charter** adopted at the **5th summit, Colombo (30 March 2022)**.
- **6th summit: Bangkok, 4 April 2025** — **Bangladesh took over the chairmanship** (Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus).

## Other groupings
- **D-8** (Developing-8 Muslim countries): founded **1997**, Istanbul; members include Bangladesh, Egypt, Indonesia, Iran, Malaysia, Nigeria, Pakistan, Turkey.
- **Climate Vulnerable Forum (CVF):** Bangladesh chaired it **2020–2022**.
- **ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF):** Bangladesh joined in **2006**.

## UN Peacekeeping (শান্তিরক্ষা) 🔥🔥
- **First participation:** **1988**, **UNIIMOG** (**Iran–Iraq**) with **15 army observers**.
- **Police** first joined in **1989** (**UNTAG, Namibia**).
- Bangladesh is consistently among the **top troop- and police-contributing countries** (often **first or second**).
- **First all-female Formed Police Unit** from Bangladesh: deployed to **Haiti (2010)**.
- **Sierra Leone** declared **Bangla** an honorary official language (**2002**) in gratitude to Bangladeshi peacekeepers.
- Training centre: **BIPSOT** (Bangladesh Institute of Peace Support Operation Training), **Rajendrapur, Gazipur**.
- **International Day of UN Peacekeepers:** **29 May**.

> 🔄 Update: check Bangladesh's current rank among UN troop contributors and the number of peacekeepers deployed.

## Quick revision
- UN: **17 Sept 1974**, **136th** member; Mujib's Bangla speech **25 Sept 1974**.
- UNSC terms: **1979–80, 2000–01**; UNGA President **Humayun Rasheed Choudhury (1986)**.
- OIC: joined **1974**, Lahore; IUT in **Gazipur**.
- SAARC: **8 Dec 1985, Dhaka**; idea of **Ziaur Rahman**; HQ **Kathmandu**; 8th member **Afghanistan**.
- BIMSTEC: **6 June 1997, Bangkok**; **7** members; HQ **Dhaka**; Bangladesh chair from **April 2025**.

## Principles of foreign policy 🔥🔥
- Guiding motto: **"সকলের সাথে বন্ধুত্ব, কারো সাথে বৈরিতা নয়" (Friendship to all, malice towards none)**.
- **Article 25** of the Constitution sets the principles: respect for national sovereignty and equality, **non-interference** in internal affairs, **peaceful settlement** of disputes, respect for **international law and the UN Charter**, support for oppressed peoples, and **general and complete disarmament**.
- Other themes: economic diplomacy, labour migration and remittance, climate diplomacy, UN peacekeeping, and a **balanced relationship** with major powers.
- The **Ministry of Foreign Affairs** is at Segunbagicha, Dhaka; diplomats are trained at the **Foreign Service Academy**.

## Rohingya crisis (রোহিঙ্গা সংকট) 🔥🔥
### Background
- The **Rohingya** are a mostly Muslim minority from **Rakhine State (old name Arakan)** of **Myanmar**.
- Myanmar's **1982 Citizenship Law** did not recognise them, leaving them **stateless**.
- Bangladesh officially calls them **"Forcibly Displaced Myanmar Nationals" (FDMN)**, not refugees, because it is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention.

### Waves of influx
| Year | About |
|---|---|
| **1978** | About 2 lakh (most returned) |
| **1991–92** | About 2.5 lakh |
| **From 25 August 2017** | About **7 lakh+** fled a military crackdown — the largest influx |

- Today about **1.1–1.3 million** Rohingya live in Bangladesh.
- Camps: **Ukhiya and Teknaf upazilas, Cox's Bazar**. **Kutupalong** is described as the **world's largest refugee camp**.
- **Bhasan Char (ভাসানচর), Noakhali:** relocation began in **December 2020**; built with the Bangladesh Navy.
- **Repatriation Arrangement** with Myanmar: signed **23 November 2017** (Naypyidaw). No large-scale repatriation has happened so far.

### International justice
- **ICJ (International Court of Justice):** **The Gambia v. Myanmar** genocide case filed in **November 2019** (on behalf of the OIC); **provisional measures ordered on 23 January 2020**.
- **ICC (International Criminal Court):** authorised an investigation in **November 2019** (crimes partly committed on Bangladeshi soil, since Bangladesh is an ICC member). In **November 2024** the ICC Prosecutor sought an **arrest warrant for Myanmar's military chief Min Aung Hlaing**.
- **Argentina** also opened a universal-jurisdiction case.

### Recent situation (as of 2025)
- Fighting between Myanmar's army and the **Arakan Army** has put most of Rakhine, including the border area, under Arakan Army control; new arrivals entered Bangladesh in **2024–25**.
- Funding cuts to humanitarian aid have reduced food rations in the camps.
- The UN held a **high-level conference on the Rohingya** during the UN General Assembly in **September 2025**.

> 🔄 Update: check the latest Rohingya population figure (UNHCR), repatriation talks, ICJ/ICC progress and any new UN resolutions.

## Blue economy (সুনীল অর্থনীতি) 🔥🔥
- Meaning: using **ocean and sea resources** for economic growth, jobs and better livelihoods **while keeping the ocean healthy**.
- The term is linked to Belgian economist **Gunter Pauli** (book *The Blue Economy*, 2010).
- Bangladesh's sea area after the **2012 (Myanmar)** and **2014 (India)** verdicts: about **1,18,813 sq km** (territorial sea, EEZ and continental shelf) — see BD-25.
- **Blue Economy Cell** (2017) coordinates the work (under the Energy and Mineral Resources Division).
- Related SDG: **SDG 14 – Life below water**.

### Sectors
| Sector | Examples |
|---|---|
| Fisheries & aquaculture | Deep-sea fishing, marine fish, seaweed |
| Energy | **Offshore oil and gas** blocks, wind and tidal power |
| Shipping & ports | Chattogram, Mongla, Payra, **Matarbari** deep-sea port; shipbuilding |
| Minerals | **Heavy mineral sand** (Cox's Bazar), salt |
| Tourism | Cox's Bazar (**longest unbroken natural sea beach**, about 120 km), Kuakata, St Martin's |
| Marine biotechnology | Medicines, cosmetics from marine life |

### Marine protected areas
- **Swatch of No Ground (সোয়াচ অব নো গ্রাউন্ড):** a deep **submarine canyon** in the Bay of Bengal; home of dolphins, whales and sharks. Declared Bangladesh's **first Marine Protected Area** in **2014**.
- **Nijhum Dwip** marine area and **St Martin's** are also protected.
- **Kuakata (Patuakhali)** is called **"সাগরকন্যা"** — both sunrise and sunset can be seen from the beach.

## Climate change (জলবায়ু পরিবর্তন) 🔥🔥
- Bangladesh is one of the **most climate-vulnerable countries** (low, flat delta; cyclones; floods; salinity; sea-level rise).
- A **1 metre sea-level rise** could flood about **17%** of the land (commonly cited figure).
- **Germanwatch Global Climate Risk Index 2021:** Bangladesh **7th** most affected country (2000–2019).

### Policies and funds 🔥
| Policy / fund | Year | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **NAPA** (National Adaptation Programme of Action) | **2005** | First adaptation plan |
| **BCCSAP** (Bangladesh Climate Change Strategy and Action Plan) | **2009** | 6 pillars |
| **Bangladesh Climate Change Trust Fund (BCCTF)** | **2009–10** | Among the first **national climate funds financed from a country's own budget** |
| **Climate Change Trust Act** | **2010** | |
| **National Adaptation Plan (NAP) 2023–2050** | **2022** | Submitted to UNFCCC |
| **Updated NDC** | **2021** | Emission-reduction targets under the Paris Agreement |
| **Mujib Climate Prosperity Plan** | **2022** | Climate prosperity roadmap to 2041 |

- Bangladesh chaired the **Climate Vulnerable Forum (CVF)** and V20 in **2020–2022**.
- **Global Center on Adaptation** opened its **South Asia office in Dhaka** (2020).

### Global climate milestones
| Event | Key fact |
|---|---|
| **UNFCCC** | Adopted **1992** (Rio Earth Summit) |
| **Kyoto Protocol** | **1997** |
| **Paris Agreement (COP21)** | **2015**; keep warming well below **2 °C**, aim for **1.5 °C** |
| **Loss and Damage Fund** | Agreed at **COP27, Sharm el-Sheikh (2022)** |
| **COP29** | **Baku, Azerbaijan (2024)** — new climate finance goal |
| **COP30** | **Belém, Brazil (November 2025)** |
| **Green Climate Fund** | HQ **Songdo, South Korea** |

> 🔄 Update: note the outcome of the latest COP and Bangladesh's latest rank in the Climate Risk Index.

## Bangladesh Delta Plan 2100 (বাংলাদেশ ব-দ্বীপ পরিকল্পনা ২১০০) 🔥🔥
- Approved by the **NEC (National Economic Council)** on **4 September 2018**.
- Prepared by the **General Economics Division (GED), Planning Commission**, with help from the **Netherlands**.
- A **long-term (100-year) techno-economic plan** for water, climate, food security and environment.
- **Investment target:** about **2.5% of GDP** per year; **80 projects** in the first phase (to 2030).
- **3 higher-level (national) goals** and **6 specific goals**.
- **6 hotspots (হটস্পট):**
  1. **Coastal zone (উপকূলীয় অঞ্চল)** — the largest hotspot
  2. **Barind and drought-prone areas**
  3. **Haor and flash-flood areas**
  4. **Chattogram Hill Tracts**
  5. **River systems and estuaries**
  6. **Urban areas**
- Model: the Netherlands' own **Delta Programme**.

- Delta Plan 2100 approved **4 Sept 2018**; **6 hotspots**; partner **Netherlands**; **2.5% of GDP**.

> **Why it matters:** Questions on the July–August 2024 mass uprising, the interim government, the reform commissions and the road to the 13th parliamentary election are now standard in BCS and all government job exams, including the viva.

## Background: the quota reform movement 🔥
- In **2018** the government abolished quotas in 9th–13th grade government jobs after student protests.
- On **5 June 2024** the **High Court** declared that 2018 circular illegal, bringing back the **30% freedom-fighter quota**.
- Students began protests in **early July 2024** under the banner **"বৈষম্যবিরোধী ছাত্র আন্দোলন" (Students Against Discrimination)**, with programmes such as **"বাংলা ব্লকেড"**.

## July–August 2024 mass uprising (জুলাই গণ-অভ্যুত্থান) 🔥🔥
| Date (2024) | Event |
|---|---|
| **16 July** | **আবু সাঈদ**, a student of **Begum Rokeya University, Rangpur**, was shot dead by police; he became the symbol of the movement |
| **18 July** onward | "Complete shutdown" programme; mobile and broadband **internet shut down** across the country |
| **19–20 July** | **Curfew** imposed; army deployed |
| **21 July** | **Appellate Division** verdict: **93% merit**, **5%** freedom fighters' children/grandchildren, **1%** ethnic minorities, **1%** persons with disabilities and third gender |
| **3 August** | At the **Central Shaheed Minar**, the movement announced a **one-point demand**: the government's resignation |
| **5 August** | "**March to Dhaka**"; Prime Minister **Sheikh Hasina resigned and left for India**. Supporters call the day **"৩৬ জুলাই"** |
| **6 August** | President **Mohammed Shahabuddin** **dissolved the 12th Jatiya Sangsad** |
| **8 August** | **Interim government** sworn in at **Bangabhaban**, with **Dr Muhammad Yunus** as **Chief Adviser (প্রধান উপদেষ্টা)** |

- The **UN Human Rights Office (OHCHR)** fact-finding report (**February 2025**) estimated that **up to about 1,400 people** may have been killed between 15 July and 5 August 2024, many of them young people and children.

## The interim government (অন্তর্বর্তীকালীন সরকার) 🔥🔥
- **Chief Adviser:** **Dr Muhammad Yunus** (Nobel Peace Prize 2006).
- Two student coordinators, **Nahid Islam** and **Asif Mahmud Shojib Bhuyain**, joined as advisers. Nahid Islam later resigned (February 2025) to lead the new **National Citizen Party (NCP)**, launched on **28 February 2025**.
- Legal basis: an advisory opinion of the **Appellate Division** (Article 106 reference) supported the formation.
- New key office-holders in August 2024 included Chief Justice **Syed Refaat Ahmed** and Bangladesh Bank Governor **Ahsan H. Mansur**; the Army Chief was **General Waker-Uz-Zaman**.
- **Chief Election Commissioner:** **A. M. M. Nasir Uddin** (appointed **November 2024**).
- Budget FY2025–26 (Tk 7.90 lakh crore) was presented on television by Finance Adviser **Dr Salehuddin Ahmed** (see BD-29).

## Reform commissions (সংস্কার কমিশন) 🔥🔥
The first **six commissions** were announced on **11 September 2024**:

| Commission | Head |
|---|---|
| **Constitution Reform** | **অধ্যাপক আলী রীয়াজ** |
| **Electoral System Reform** | **ড. বদিউল আলম মজুমদার** |
| **Judiciary Reform** | **Justice Shah Abu Nayeem Mominur Rahman** |
| **Police Reform** | **Safar Raj Hossain** |
| **Anti-Corruption Commission Reform** | **ড. ইফতেখারুজ্জামান** |
| **Public Administration Reform** | **Abdul Muyeed Chowdhury** |

- Later commissions covered **media, health, labour, women's affairs and local government**, making **11** in all.
- The first commissions submitted their reports in **January–February 2025**.
- **National Consensus Commission (জাতীয় ঐকমত্য কমিশন):** formed in **February 2025** to build agreement among parties on the reform proposals. **Chair: Muhammad Yunus**; **Vice-chair: Ali Riaz**.
- The result was the **July National Charter (জুলাই জাতীয় সনদ)**, signed by most political parties in **October 2025**. A **referendum** on it was planned together with the national election.
- In **May 2025** the interim government **banned all activities of the Awami League** under the Anti-Terrorism Act, pending trials, and the Election Commission suspended its registration.

## The 13th parliamentary election (ত্রয়োদশ জাতীয় সংসদ নির্বাচন)
- The Election Commission announced the schedule in **December 2025**, fixing the vote for **12 February 2026**, **on the same day as the referendum** on the July Charter.
